name: Pyruvic acid peel

lead: Pyruvic acid peels are superficial chemical peels applied in a clinic, mostly for acne. People book them to clear breakouts and refresh dull, congested skin.

Pyruvic acid is a keratolytic alpha-keto acid that loosens the outer skin layers so they shed, which clears pores and eases breakouts. Published work is small: a 2014 comparison of 50% pyruvic and 30% salicylic acid peels in 20 acne patients measured effects on facial sebum secretion.

paras: A clinician applies it in the office, and treatment is usually repeated as a series. Mild peeling follows, and sunscreen is used afterward.
Peels in general can cause redness, photosensitivity, pigment change and, rarely, scarring.

angle.text: People book pyruvic acid peels to clear active acne and refresh dull, congested skin. The keratolytic acid sheds the outer layer so pores clear and breakouts ease. A handful of small studies cover its use in acne.

lead: A pyruvic acid peel is a clinic-applied chemical peel that uses pyruvic acid, an alpha-keto acid, to loosen and shed the outer layers of skin. People have it done to reduce active acne, soften acne scars, even out pigmentation such as melasma, and improve skin texture, so skin looks clearer and smoother.[1][2][3][4][5]

Pyruvic acid is described as keratolytic, antimicrobial and sebostatic, and a 2006 study reports it can stimulate collagen and elastic fiber formation. Because it is small and has a low pKa it penetrates quickly, and a peel typically causes intense burning followed by redness, flaking and sometimes crusting.[4]
Published evidence consists of small clinical studies, mostly 20 to 60 participants, covering acne, acne scars, melasma and photodamage.[1][2][3][4][5]
infobox: Sessions every 2 weeks for 8 to 12 weeks[2][3]

paras: Pyruvic acid is grouped with the superficial peeling agents, alongside alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic acid and beta hydroxy acids such as salicylic acid.[5][6] Chemical peels as a class are used for fine lines, acne, acne scars and pigment changes. Wikipedia describes light peels as AHA and BHA peels done in offices or med spas, and medium-depth peels such as TCA as needing a medical provider.[6]
A 2022 study states pyruvic acid at 40 to 70 percent is used as a superficial to medium peeling agent.[2]

Pyruvic acid application usually causes intense burning, and the post-peel period involves redness, desquamation and sometimes crusting.[4] Chemical peels of all strengths can cause photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigmentary changes, milia, skin atrophy and scarring, according to Wikipedia.[6] Study exclusion criteria included a history of hypertrophic scarring, keloids and active or recurrent herpes.[2]
Pyruvic acid peels appear in looksmaxxing taxonomies as one of the clinic-based skin-resurfacing options in the hardmaxx category.

Acne: a 2014 study of 20 patients aged 13 to 30 compared a 50% pyruvic acid peel (10 patients) with a 30% salicylic acid peel (10 patients) and measured facial sebum secretion.[5] A 2022 study of 30 people with acne, post-acne scarring and hyperpigmentation gave 40% pyruvic acid peels every two weeks for 12 weeks and recorded a significant fall in comedones and papules.[2]

Acne scars: a 2023 randomized split-face trial of 30 patients compared microneedling with 15% TCA against microneedling with 25% pyruvic acid. Scar scores improved on both sides with no significant difference between them.[1]

Melasma: a 2025 trial randomized 60 patients to 90% lactic acid or 40% pyruvic acid peels every two weeks for 12 weeks; MASI scores fell from about 9.65 to 4.53 in the pyruvic acid group, similar to the lactic acid group.[3]
Photodamage: a 2006 study of 20 subjects tested a new 50% pyruvic acid formulation in four sessions two weeks apart for photodamage, superficial scarring and melasma.[4]
